solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique, linked answer split by the grid); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Claimed ESP, but putting one’s foot down

blocks.note: 'though' can replace 'but' to introduce a contrast
to tread is to put your foot down as you walk

explanation.surface: Someone boasted of extrasensory powers while also standing firm on some matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Putting one's foot down' suggests being firm, but here it is literal walking. Note the word break in the wordplay falls one letter away from the break in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Supposedly knowing what another person is thinking is the classic example of a claimed psychic or extrasensory ability.

clue.text: See 8
R&A accepting electronic clubs in Open panic?

indicators.note: to accept something is to take it in, so one piece goes inside another
'in' places what precedes it inside what follows

blocks.note: the letters of the golf body's abbreviation, the Royal and Ancient
E is the standard abbreviation for electronic, as in e-mail
C is the abbreviation for clubs in card games
overt means open, done without concealment

explanation.surface: Golf's governing body is in a flap about electronic clubs being used at the Open championship.
explanation.walkthrough: R&A takes in E to make REA, then C is added, and REAC goes inside OVERT. 'Open' looks like the golf tournament but means not hidden.
explanation.definitionFit: To panic is to respond far more strongly than a situation warrants, which is exactly what reacting excessively means.

clue.text: Enjoyable German channel

blocks.note: first meaning: the German word for good
second meaning: a narrow passage of water, or the intestinal tube

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a review of a German TV channel; really the German word for 'good' and a word for a narrow channel happen to be spelt the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Gut is German for good, close to enjoyable, and in English a gut is a narrow strait or the alimentary passage.

clue.text: Tevye’s original player, object lesson for beginners

indicators.note: beginners are starters, so only the opening letter of each word is wanted

blocks.note: the initial letters of these five words

explanation.surface: A theatre note: the first actor to play Tevye taught newcomers a model lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition words also supply three of the initials, so the clue partly describes itself. Tevye is the milkman hero of the musical Fiddler on the Roof.
explanation.definitionFit: The Israeli actor created the role of the milkman in the first London production and starred in the 1971 film.

clue.text: Green car secured by this chap trading online

indicators.note: something secured by another is held fast inside it

blocks.note: eco- is the prefix for environmentally green things
short for a Mercedes
the setter referring to himself

explanation.surface: An eco-friendly car is being protected by a man who does business over the internet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This chap' is the setter speaking of himself, a common crossword way of giving the first-person pronoun. 'Green' is not a colour here but environmental.
explanation.definitionFit: Buying and selling goods over the internet is the standard meaning of the electronic-commerce term.

clue.text: Have case of toner left over in study crushed

indicators.note: a case is the outside casing, so only the outermost letters are kept
'in' puts the preceding material inside the next piece

blocks.note: to own something is to have it
first and last letters of the word
an odd one is left over when the rest are paired
a den is a private room for working

explanation.surface: Someone owns leftover printer toner in their study and is feeling crushed by it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case of' is a common way to ask for a word's outer letters. 'Left over' reads as a description of the toner, but it supplies its own piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Oppressed people are described as trampled underfoot, so crushed and downtrodden share the sense of being kept down by force.

clue.text: Shark tender

blocks.note: first meaning: a species of bottom-dwelling shark
second meaning: one who tends the sick

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shark tender' looks like a single odd phrase, perhaps someone who looks after sharks; it is two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The nurse shark is a slow sea fish, and a tender is someone who tends or cares for patients.

clue.text: Progress, it’s not shown by 1A; 22 & 24

annotation.answer: ONE STEP FORWARD TWO STEPS BACK

blocks.note: surface reading: a gloomy verdict that something is not really advancing
setter's reading: 1A has TREAD running forwards across its two words, while 22 and 24 each have PACE written backwards across theirs

explanation.surface: A pessimist complains that some much-touted advance is no advance at all, citing other entries as evidence.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-references are literal: [though]T READ[ing] shows one tread going forwards; [jos]E CAP[ablanca] and [ventur]E CAP[ital] each show a pace going backwards, so two steps back. The phrase is also the title of a 1904 Lenin pamphlet.
explanation.definitionFit: Advancing a little and then retreating twice as far leaves you worse off, so the saying describes setbacks disguised as improvement.

clue.text: May Allah bless flourishing Bar Academy congregation room

indicators.note: 'bar' as a preposition means except, so something is left out
to flourish is to wave about with a showy flurry, so the letters are tossed into new order

blocks.note: taken as written, thirteen letters
A is a standard abbreviation for academy

explanation.surface: A greeting offered to a thriving Bar Academy, perhaps an Islamic law school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar Academy' looks like a legal institution, but 'Bar' means without and 'Academy' is just A. Remove one A and rearrange the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A school or institution gathers its members in a large room for meetings, worship or announcements, so a congregation room fits.

clue.text: Brusque employee’s retrieving boxes after retirement

indicators.note: to box something is to enclose it, so the wanted letters sit inside the words
retiring is withdrawing, going backwards, so the letters run the other way

blocks.note: the letters spanning the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A worker who has retired keeps fetching boxes and is curt about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boxes' reads as the thing being retrieved; it is the hiding signal, and 'retirement' turns the hidden letters round.
explanation.definitionFit: A curt, short manner of speaking is both brusque and terse; the two adjectives are close synonyms.

clue.text: Earl later rents out The Big Sleep?

indicators.note: 'out' suggests things put out of place or disordered

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for earl
taken as written

explanation.surface: A nobleman eventually lets out a famous film noir, as if hiring out a DVD.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Big Sleep' is a Raymond Chandler novel and Bogart film, but here it is taken literally as a euphemism; the question mark flags that.
explanation.definitionFit: Death is often softened as an everlasting sleep, and the phrase in funeral prayers names that final repose.

clue.text: Somebody this toned?

blocks.note: surface reading: asking about a body worked out to an extreme degree
setter's reading: strip the outer letters, the limits, from this word and ONE is left, and 'one' means somebody

explanation.surface: A gym-goer is asked whether anyone could really be this muscular.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a reverse clue: treat the answer as an instruction. Applied to 'toned' it removes the first and last letters, leaving ONE, which is 'somebody'.
explanation.definitionFit: Without its boundary letters, the word becomes a pronoun meaning a person, so the answer is the instruction that turns one into the other.

clue.text: Make smooth tree smoother

blocks.note: first meaning: to shave a wooden surface level
second meaning: the broad-leaved tree common in London streets
third meaning: the carpenter's tool that does the shaving

explanation.walkthrough: Three meanings in a row: a verb, a tree and a tool. 'Smoother' looks like a comparative adjective but is a noun, a thing that smooths.
explanation.definitionFit: A carpenter uses a bladed hand tool to level timber, the verb names that action, and the plane tree is a common shade tree.

clue.text: Keep with what is quoted for doing any work at all

blocks.note: a keep is the stronghold of a castle
'of' can mean with, as in a person of means

blocks.clueFragment: what is quoted for doing any work
blocks.note: a fee is the price quoted for a job

explanation.surface: Someone holds on to the quote they were given before they would lift a finger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keep' looks like a verb but is the castle tower. The idiom is British: someone who 'can't sing for toffee' can't sing at all.
explanation.definitionFit: The British idiom is used in negatives to mean in the slightest degree, so it can replace the phrase in such sentences.

clue.text: Your money back if your Dodgem was defective?

definitions.text: Your money back if your Dodgem was defective?

blocks.clueFragment: Your money back if your Dodgem was defective?
blocks.note: surface reading: a customer complaint about a broken bumper car and a refund
setter's reading: dodgems are a funfair ride, so a funfair that refunds you is being just, and the stock phrase for a call to be just doubles as a description of it

explanation.surface: At the funfair your bumper car broke down, and you expect a refund.
explanation.walkthrough: Dodgems are the electric bumper cars at a travelling fair. The answer is the phrase people say when appealing to fairness, read here as 'the funfair is fair'.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means everyone should be treated justly, which is exactly the principle behind refunding a ride that failed.

clue.text: Stoke welcomes news, having cleared eel-catcher?

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: to stoke a fire is to fuel it
N is new, so 'news' is two of them
money cleared after deductions is net

explanation.surface: Stoke, perhaps the Potteries town, is glad to hear an eel-catcher has been removed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'News' is cheekily read as the plural of 'new', giving two Ns. 'Cleared' is the net sum after costs, not something removed.
explanation.definitionFit: A cone-shaped trap net that guides fish into a narrowing mouth is used for catching eels, so this is an example, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Fear independent singer suppresses during gathering

indicators.note: to suppress is to hold something down within, so one piece is held inside
something happening during an event sits within it

blocks.note: I is the abbreviation for independent
a tenor is a male singer
a bee is a social gathering, as in a sewing bee

explanation.surface: A fearful independent singer keeps quiet at a gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: There are two containers nested one inside the other. A 'bee' as a gathering, as in a spelling bee or sewing bee, is the less obvious meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means a person or thing one especially dreads or loathes, an object of fear and dislike.

clue.text: Play the hooligan in Scottish Play for returning star?

indicators.note: to return is to come back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: to play a part is to be it, as in 'be the villain'
ned is Scottish slang for a young hooligan

explanation.surface: An actor in Macbeth, the 'Scottish Play', plays a thug and gets a return engagement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scottish Play' is the theatre name for Macbeth, but 'in Scottish' simply flags the Scots slang word; the second 'Play' belongs only to the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: The bright white star in the constellation Cygnus is a named star, one of the Summer Triangle.

clue.text: Chronicles mock Israeli monarch

indicators.note: a mock version is a fake, not the real arrangement, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: Ch is the abbreviation for the biblical book of Chronicles
taken as written

explanation.surface: Biblical histories poke fun at a king of Israel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Israeli monarch' looks like one phrase pointing to David or Solomon; in fact 'Israeli' is the anagram material and 'monarch' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The Restoration king of England, Scotland and Ireland, nicknamed the Merry Monarch, reigned from 1660 to 1685.

clue.text: Pay agreed

blocks.note: first meaning: make amends, pay for a wrong
second meaning: split as two words, in full agreement

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a wage deal. The second meaning needs the answer split as AT ONE, meaning in agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: To make amends for a sin is to pay for it, and people in harmony are said to be at one.

clue.text: It’s admitted by leading light — he fathered twins

indicators.note: someone admitted is let inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: 'it' is old slang for sex appeal, SA
I (one, number one) plus AC, read as ace: a top performer

explanation.surface: A tribute to a pioneering figure, revealed as a father of twins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' meaning sex appeal comes from the 1920s Clara Bow film; the 's is just the verb. The leading-light piece is loose: '1 AC' as a number-one ace.
explanation.definitionFit: In Genesis the patriarch and his wife Rebekah had the twin sons Esau and Jacob, so the description identifies him.

clue.text: Like kid in workhouse maybe, in seven days asking for seconds

indicators.note: seconds are second items, so every second letter is the one kept

blocks.note: every second letter of the three words run together

explanation.surface: Oliver Twist, the workhouse boy, keeps asking for more food for a whole week.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Asking for seconds' recalls Oliver Twist's 'Please, sir, I want some more'. Take every second letter of 'in seven days'.
explanation.definitionFit: A child in a workhouse would be poor and in want, so lacking necessities fits, with 'maybe' marking it as an example.

clue.text: As Palace job can hurt former top man on board

indicators.note: something hurt is damaged, knocked out of shape

blocks.note: taken as written, fourteen letters

explanation.surface: Working at the Palace, perhaps Crystal Palace football club, can damage an ex-boss of the board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On board' suggests a company boardroom; it is the chessboard. Crystal Palace is a London football club.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cuban grandmaster held the world chess championship from 1921 to 1927, so he was once the leading player on the board.

clue.text: Perhaps take some water round

blocks.note: first meaning: drink with the tongue, as a cat or dog does
second meaning: one circuit of a track

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a trip round a lake; 'perhaps' warns that drinking water is just one example of the action.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals drink by flicking liquid up with the tongue, and one complete circuit of a racetrack is called the same.

clue.text: To sum it up: in future, what’s up front can be lost

definitions.text: To sum it up: in future, what’s up front can be lost

indicators.text: what’s up front can be lost
indicators.note: the front letter is allowed to drop away
'in' places what precedes it inside what follows

blocks.note: to sum up is to recap, followed by 'it' as written
eventual means future, here losing its opening letter

explanation.surface: A summary of investing: money put up front might be gone later.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: RECAP IT goes inside [e]VENTUAL, and read straight, the clue describes risky investment money.
explanation.definitionFit: Investors fund young businesses up front knowing the stake may never be recovered, which is what risk funding for start-ups means.
